item.title: Spinners, weavers, and the future of data work
item.description:
When I first started working with big data sets in the 2010s, the analogy being thrown around was that data mining was like digging for oil. Around that time large organizations (and biological scientists using cheap next-generation sequencing) had figured out that having immense amounts of data was valuable, but they needed someone to turn that raw data into value, competitive advantage, insights, or answers to questions, etc.

What this analogy misses is that there are two distinct steps to the production pipeline going from crude oil (data) to the fully refined product (insights). I thought it might be better served by another analogy paired with a historical example, one that can provide clues for predicting the shape of data work in this new age of AI.

The spinners and the weavers of the industrial revolution

For those who aren’t all that crafty (like myself), here’s a history lesson and some background on how you make cloth. The British textile industry of the 1700s involved the prototypical “cottage industry,” with a workforce made up mostly of women serving in two different roles along the path from raw cotton to finished cloth. First, the cotton fibers had to be spun into yarn. This was done by the spinners, who for centuries were women who worked from home in their spare time. This yarn was the raw material, the thread, that then could be used by hand weavers on a loom to create full pieces of cloth. It’s the weavers who are most often cited in technological automation stories told by historians, as their roles were automated out of existence by the powerlooms of large factories, but the replacement of the spinners actually occurred first. It was just not studied, because it primarily affected women.

Okay, cool history, but what does this all have to do with data?

Spinning is a lot like the quality control, upstream processing, and basic data cleaning that has to happen at the start of any data project. It results in the processed data products that can be used, woven if you will, into helpful insights. Around the 18th and 19th centuries both the spinners and the weavers endured a period of intense technological change. New technologies fundamentally changed or disrupted their profession, much like the effects being experienced right now by those working with data, coding, and AI.

From 1765 to 1779, three new technological inventions (the spinning jenny, the water frame, and the spinning mule) made spinning dramatically more efficient and automated. This did two things: 1) over the next few decades the number of cottage spinners declined rapidly,1 putting hand spinners out of work almost entirely by the 1830s, and 2) it led to a massive amount of cheap yarn available for weaving. This, in turn, created a brief “golden age” for the hand weavers, with their numbers peaking in 1820 before the powerloom ultimately put them all out of work by the 1860s.

A thoroughly depressing story in today’s context, isn’t it? So what can we learn from it?

There’s still time to be a weaver

You’ll notice that in the case of the textile industry the technology started upstream and then gradually moved the bottleneck further down the path, from the spinners and then to the weavers. The glut of cheap yarn even encouraged the growth of the weaving industry for many years before it too succumbed to automation.

Many of us in the data business have had to play both of these roles at one time or another: cleaning data, constructing pipelines, and running analyses, but also asking questions of them to derive insights, constructing narratives from the data, and conveying them to stakeholders (or in research papers in academia). There’s no question that today’s AI, as of this moment, is capable of massively automating and expediting the first set, the spinning. But it’s less clear that our current AI models can handle the more nebulous problems associated with data weaving. In fact, recent highly specialized benchmarks in the biology field suggest that even the leading models get to the correct answer on complex “omics” problems less than 45% of the time.2 Superintelligent AI might eventually be able to take the place of the powerloom and automate humans out of the entire workflow, but until then there is still time to be a good weaver. In the case of Britain it actually took a few business cycles of boom and bust to send off the weavers for good.3

One could argue that it might be the best time ever to be a data weaver, given how much of the tedious work that once fell on our plate can now be automated. We’ll all soon be drowning in yarn! The trick will be learning to work with and assess the quality of the new raw materials generated by our AI counterparts. Knowing your domain (the biology in computational bio) was always part of the weaving process, but now it’s more important than ever. As it stands right now, I still believe that human expertise can help fill the gap in the benchmarks for both spinning and weaving tasks. This could happen in a few different ways: at small scale there are human-in-the-loop checks, but I think there’s also a place for human-designed pipelines directing (constraining?) the randomness of AIs to the “correct” path set down by a real expert. These new “AI pipelines” can scale no matter how much data you have.

I’m building all of these ideas into a special kind of AI harness I’m calling Stringency. The idea is that the right pulls of human attention into the loop, along with automated controls of important data processing steps, paired with the fast, flexible research and coding expertise of AI, can lead to more (and more reproducible) science for all of us.

Next up… the commandments I promised last post…

Footnotes

  1. Benjamin Schneider, “A historical episode of job-destroying technology: technological unemployment in the British Industrial Revolution”, Past & Present.↩︎

  2. “OmicsBench v1: a Latch meta-benchmark”, Latch Bio.↩︎

  3. Clark Nardinelli, “Technology and Unemployment: The Case of the Handloom Weavers”, Southern Economic Journal 53 (1986).↩︎

item.title: All scientists can run analysis pipelines now
item.description:
One thing that I have been a little bit excited about recently is a new tool I’m calling stringency. It’s basically a belay device and top rope safety harness system for scientists using AI to automate their data analysis. I’m building it to help my lab members run the correct bioinformatic analysis on new data, where correct here implies that whatever the AI does is grounded in sound, commonly accepted analysis techniques and results in completely reproducible/traceable work, no matter who is running it.

Lab biologists should run the analysis

The fact is with today’s leading AI models you can do most any bioinformatic work without knowing a single thing about writing code. This is not a bad thing! It’s only been in the last few decades as the sheer scale of genome-wide measurments began to require dedicated skillsets in running computers to analyze them that scientists (like me) began to specialize. A divide formed between “dry” and “wet” lab roles. Wet lab biologists spent their time optimizing lab protocols, or designing experiments to generate data. When they needed data analyzed that couldn’t fit in your typical excel spreadsheet they turned to their dry lab counterparts who trained in things like multiple testing correction and analysis pipeline engineering. Today, AI’s ability to write working code in seconds has handed wet lab scientists back all the tools they need to analyze their largeest, most complex datasets from the very start to finished product. Perhaps someday robotic lab equipment and automation will do the same for us dry lab folks…but that’s for another post.

At the risk of alienating all my computational colleagues I’d argue that biologists thinking deeply about their scientific questions and collecting the data are in fact the best suited to be running the analysis through AI themselves. They have the deep domain knowledge that any generalist model will inevitably lack, and they can use it to cut through the professional-sounding noise that a model often produces when given an unfocused task or ill-formed question. Scientists are, in fact, speifically trained to ask strong, focused, and verifiable questions. Coincidentally, this is exactly what an AI needs to be given in order to help produce helpful results in the process of data analysis. What’s more, scientists know their data best. Giving them the tools to successfully analyze a dataset from start to finish avoids the dilution or “thrown over the wall” problem that plagues current collaborations where the norm is outsourcing this work to separate team members or worse…a core service group.

AI alone is a poor fit for science

But AI models with their stochastic, overly-confident nature and their transient lifespan can be unpredictable. They are by definition not reproducible which doesn’t sit well with how we do scientific work. Computational analysis, much like work in the lab, needs to be documented in a way that anyone could replicate it, it has to be reproducible. So what happens if your AI agent approaches a data anlysis problem you gave it in an unusual or unconventional way when faced with an initial roadblock, cutting a few corners but still producing something that looks and sounds like it could be correct? Or maybe an agent successfully processes your data, but then the session ends and all trace of how the outputs were generated is lost with the model’s death. Or worse, what if the agent asserts something about your data driven entirely by a hallucination and then builds off of that for the next few hours wasting everyone’s tokens, time, and grant money. You look at the spreadsheet it generated at the end and the numbers are completely wrong, or maybe you can’t even tell. At this point there is no way to answer the question: how did you do this? And without the knowledge of an experienced analyst it’s also very hard to answer the question why did you do it this way?

Scientists need a way to leverage the automation, the strong logical thinking and the significant programming ability AI brings to the table. But it needs to be in a way that is guided and constrained so that even those with no coding or technical knowledge of the underlying analysis work can drive the work forward in a responsible way.

The Commandments of Bioinformatic Agentic Pipelines

In the next few posts I’ll be introducing what I call the “Commandments of Bioinformatic Agentic Pipelines”. These are simple rules for how to use AI and autonomous agents in biological research and data analysis in a way that hopefully minimizes the risks I outlined above to reproducibility and reliability. My field is biology so I’ll be rooting things there, but much of what I’ll discuss is probably applicable to the wider research community.

Stringency is what I’m calling the engine that I’m building to force LLM models to hold to these principles. It’s a little like the belay system used in top rope climbing. In this case the agent is doing all the climbing, and you’re the one on the ground responsible for making sure it doesn’t fall off and break anything. It’s pretty hard to do that without a pulley and some rope.

We are all still learning how to use these new rapidly evolving tools, so stick around to hear more.

item.title: Hello again, internet
item.description:
Welcome to the new site. The old one dated from early grad school and had started to feel like someone else’s homepage, so I rebuilt it from scratch — still Quarto, now with a hand-rolled theme (thanks Claude!).

This blog is where I put whatever I’m thinking about at the moment that I might want to share with the world. This post doesn’t really count, but stick around and hopefully I’ll post a thing or two soon.

A few things I’m deep in at the moment:

  • AI agent tools for bioinformatics research We all are or should be using AI to write our analysis code these days, but the inherent randomness of LLMs makes it hard to achieve our goals of reliability and reproducibility in research. I’m trying to fix that with stringency…more to come soon!
  • Segmentation benchmarking. Comparing cell segmentation algorithms for Xenium data across a multi-organ mouse atlas, and building CRISP to measure segmentation purity without ground truth.
  • Spatial pipelines. Nextflow and Seurat workflows that take Xenium runs from raw output to annotated cells reproducibly.

I don’t know what purpose blogs have anymore in this new AI-slop-soaked internet but if you’re human and reading this maybe we’ll find out.
